title: Right Livelihood
speaker: Joden Bob Rose
summary: Joden Bob Rose takes up Right Livelihood, the fifth element of the Eightfold Noble Path, drawing on Thich Nhat Hanh's The Heart of the Buddha's Teaching, the Metta Sutta, and the Buddha's image of a goldsmith holding a balance scale in the Anguttara Nikaya. Joden tells of a stepdaughter's aunt, a state prosecutor who died surrounded by hoarded purchases, then traces a path from pre-med studies through boatbuilding, forest conservation, and farmland protection. Small groups take up questions about what in their own work embodies Right Livelihood. One group reports that it is okay to say no, and a member recalls telling a boss that thinking about work in the shower is against their religion.

sentences.text: New friends, nice to see everyone.
Old friends and new faces.

A few months ago, some of us took on an assignment to take one of the Eightfold Noble Path portions and speak to that, and I chose Right Livelihood, which might also be called Ethics of Earning a Living or Conscious Livelihood.
I want to begin by acknowledging Scott Allen's presentation on the same topic a few weeks ago.
Some wires got crossed, and so we both did the same thing.
I appreciate Scott's openness to address the dilemma that he walked through of integrating Right Livelihood in the context of military service.

I listened to his talk after I had begun preparation for my assignment that I had penned months ago, so there may be a few items repeated, but hopefully I'll cover some new ground and remind us all of how central this concept of Right Livelihood is for maintaining the integrity of our lives of continuing practice in this chaotic and changing world we live in.
I'll open up with a few initial reflections, followed by a brief overview of what the Buddha offers as teachings on Right Livelihood.

I'll conclude, as Tim asked us to, with some reflections on how our personal stories, or at least my imagination of that story, provide some examples of what can be considered, I think, Right Livelihood.
Then I'd like to take a few minutes for all of us to reflect on this intersection of our practice and our day-to-day lives.
In Pali, this element is called Samo Adjivo, commonly translated as Right Livelihood.
If you dig a little bit deeper, it's clear that this term means more than a job to make money to put a roof over your head, to buy food, to have clothes and secure medicine.
In Pali, the prefix sama means complete or perfected, rather than right with all its connotations of orthodox correctness.
Samo Adjivo might better be translated more like Livelihood fully understood and rightly conducted within all the tensions of our lives.

Thich Nhat Hanh reminds us in *The Heart of the Buddha's Teaching*, the text that Desiree so beautifully guided us through, that it is not possible to practice one element of the Noble Eightfold Path without practicing all seven other elements.
This is the nature of interbeing, and it is true for all the teachings offered by the Buddha.
He continues: to practice Right Livelihood, you have to find a way to earn your living without transgressing your ideals of love and compassion.
The way you support yourself can be an expression of your deepest self, or it can be a source of suffering for you and others.
Our vocation can nourish our understanding and compassion, or erode them.
We should be awake to the consequences, far and near, of the way we earn our living.

In this perspective, another way to view Right Livelihood is to live in ways that contribute to harmony and well-being in nature and society, in our relationships with each other, and with the entire web of life.
A group of us have been studying the precepts, and I've been reminded how the Three Pure Precepts essentially offer us a high-level perspective on practicing Right Livelihood in our day-to-day lives.
Do good, avoid causing harm, and help others.
It really comes down to making our best effort, despite difficulties, moment by moment, breath by breath, to fully embody these guideposts.
As we consider Right Livelihood tonight, I'd like you to reflect on a few lines from the Metta Sutta about Right Livelihood in the context of how we live our lives in our current social context.
We chant:
*This is what should be accomplished by the one who is wise.
Let one be strenuous, upright, and sincere, without pride, easily contented, and joyous.
Let one not be submerged by the things of the world.
Let one not take on the burden of riches.
Let one's senses be controlled.
And let one be wise, but not puffed up, and let one not desire great possessions even for one's family.*
We will investigate this further.
These lines are a good reminder that it's not only a matter of how we earn our living, but also of what we do and what is affected by our securing those resources.

Then there's what we do with those resources and how we use them to present ourselves within our larger community of family, sangha, and mother earth sangha, because of our ability to access material wealth.

The eightfold path elements are not so much prescriptions for behavior as qualities, a framework present in the mind of a person on the enlightening path, committed to ending suffering for all beings.
One classic way that's used to see the structure of these eight interrelated path elements is to view them as a threefold training in ethics, concentration, and wisdom.
Ethics, or avoidance of non-virtuous deeds, through right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
Concentration, or control of the mind, through right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
And wisdom, or the development of insight into the nature of reality, as right view and right intention.
What the Buddha taught about right and wrong livelihood for the mainly rural society he lived in was prohibitory.
He said lay people shouldn't engage in five specific types of business.
Dealing in weapons.
Trade in human beings, i.e. slavery and prostitution, although some translations say trade in any beings, human and non-human.
Meat production and butchery as a trade, not as a necessity of individual survival.
Business and intoxicants, and business and poisons.

The Buddha also, when pressed vigorously on three questions asked by senior monks, cautioned against becoming a soldier, quote, because the mind is already seized, debased, and misdirected by the thought, may these beings be struck down or slaughtered or annihilated or destroyed, may they not exist.
He also cautioned against a career in acting.
Those who are bound by bonds of passion will focus with even more passion on things inspiring [unclear: "a version"] presented by an actor on stage in the midst of a festival.
I think we could have long discussions about both of these recommendations, but I'm going to move on.
In the Digya Nikaya Sutra, the Buddha extensively lays out prohibitions for monks and, by inference, for seriously practicing lay people.

It's a seemingly endless list of prohibited activities, ranging from scheming, persuading, belittling others, pursuing gain with additional gain, that is, speculative profiteering, to a whole array of fortune-telling adventures such as palmistry, reading tea leaves, interpreting falling stars, reading omens and signs on bones, frayed cloth or grains of rice gnawed by mice.
I'm not making this up.
Snake charming, etc., etc.
One way to see this array is that they are all means to forecast, to somehow predict or assure oneself of the future.
Surely a futile task and contrary to addressing what is present in this moment, but I guess monks needed to find some additional revenue to meet their personal needs not provided by the monastery.
That's a topic for another day.
Reflecting on the Metta Sutra language with respect to right livelihood, the Buddha said there's nothing wrong with making money and looking after one's family in a modest fashion.
But we must know how to make a living in a way that does not cause harm to others or ourselves.
For example, we do not engage in an occupation that involves cruelty to animals or human beings, or one that obliges us to use deception or inflict physical or mental pain on others.
If these things are involved, then we should reject that form of livelihood.
In the Anuttara Sutra, the Buddha reflects on the Middle Way when he tells disciple [unclear: "Vyajra Habaja"], *"A householder knowing his income and expenses leads a balanced life.
Neither extravagant nor miserly, knowing that thus his income will stand in excess of his expenses, but not his expenses in excess of his income."*
He uses the image of a goldsmith holding up a balance scale, who knows how much it is tilted or dipped down to know the right balance point.
Each of us is that goldsmith, monitoring our behavior, knowing when we are tilting toward imbalance, and hopefully self-correcting to keep our lives properly in balance.
Beyond a balancing of income and expense for the necessities of life is the question of one's attitude towards consumption, and how we view what we need versus our wants.
This is a deep systemic dilemma we all face every day in the context of global, exploitive, market-driven, hyper-consumer-based capitalism perfected right here in America.
And we're right in the middle of it every breath we take.

One of the Buddha's teachings is to let go of our acquisitive tendencies, which thereby weakens our temptation to engage in wrong livelihood in order to secure more than we need for reasonable comfort in our lives.
That is, to develop a disposition of contentment and acceptance of what we are given as adequate and satisfactory.

Or as Bodhidharma counsels in his outline of practice, *accept conditions and want nothing.* One consequence of this shift is to place less of a burden on the great earth that sustains us by not taking up the burden of riches and [unclear: "having our senses control"].

Taking a moment to reflect each time our mind signals a want in the face of endless temptations, many of which require a financial response, is a critical exercise in understanding what we truly need to meet our basic requirements of living as conscious lay people in this increasingly complex, technology-driven 21st century.

And as we liberate ourselves from selfishness and unmindful entanglement with this broken world, we become less selfish, more compassionate, and [unclear: "not much more capable"] of generosity, holding on to nothing.
In the same Anuttara Sutra, the master reflects:
*One tries to abandon wrong livelihood and enter into right livelihood.
This is right effort.
One is mindful to abandon wrong livelihood and enter and remain in right livelihood.
This is right mindfulness.*
These three qualities, right view, right effort, and right mindfulness, run and circle around right livelihood.
In this context, I'd like to offer a short tale of right livelihood not necessarily leading to an integrated life.
My stepdaughter's single, childless aunt recently passed away.
She was a highly paid state attorney specializing in white collar crime prosecution, basically pursuing cheaters and thieves.
We would consider that right livelihood, wouldn't we?
Well, it turns out she used her high income to buy things, not just to be comfortable, but to establish some kind of protective fortress.
In short, it turns out she was a hoarder.

Upon her passing, the house was literally packed with everything from household waste, uneaten food, and boxes upon boxes, literally to the ceiling, of mostly unopened, high priced, name brand clothing, kitchen appliances, knickknacks, and other goods.
Often there were multiple examples of the same thing.
A house full in Monteseno, an apartment in Olympia, and two offsite storage containers all jammed full.
She was found deceased in a barely accessible chair in her living room.
Truly a sad and horrific ending to what seemed to be a successful life.
But no, deep delusions were obviously at play.
A brand new, unopened Dyson vacuum cleaner had recently arrived to begin finally cleaning all of this up.
Here we have right livelihood not just submerged by the things of the world, but literally being drowned by them.
Disconnected from concepts of moderation and self care, coupled with extravagant material indulgence, mindless acquisition with no actual utilization or [unclear: "extensible purpose"].
A cautionary tale indeed about an imbalanced, unbalanced approach to living out one's life.
Part of our charge from [unclear: "Noam on Tim"] for these summer presentations was to tell our personal stories and how they interacted with and were interpenetrated by the noble eightfold path.
So now I'll tell you a personal story about finding right livelihood, or more properly, right livelihoods.

It's easy to become attached to the idea of a vocation, a single life career, and get caught over time by an old dream that doesn't necessarily yield the happiness of being able to respond to what arises.
And it's hard to trust how you feel as you mature.
Try out different endeavors and begin, or at least try your darndest, to find your personal sweet spot.

One of the great good fortunes of my life has been the succession of right livelihood doors that each opened to unexpected opportunities to build community and do my part in protecting some special place in our region on this suffering planet Earth.
In my case, from an early age, the apparent goal was to be a doctor.
Growing up in South Florida, my best friend's dad was an oral surgeon and a researcher.
So when the Soviets, Russia, the Soviet Union, launched Sputnik in 1957, some of you may remember that, there was a cry to accelerate science study.
So my friend Michael, three other students, and I began that summer a series of research internships which we each pursued for the next five years until high school graduation.
Then off to pre-med studies at Tufts University, where after a year of cruising by on advanced high school classes, I hit the wall with organic chemistry.
Also a function of 8 o'clock in the morning Saturday lectures after some serious Friday night partying.
I also realized I really didn't like my fellow pre-meds.
And I couldn't imagine two more years in which I would be able to do that.
Shifting to a major in English distressed my parents mightily, but there was no going back.
In fact, my mom, a vocational business school teacher, had me take an aptitude test.
The result was, "You can do anything you want, you just have to decide what you want to do."
So that BA was followed by a [unclear: "co-forma"] master's degree in connection to some of the major poets of that time, and landed me a job in medical school.
I co-formed a master's degree in connection to some of the major poets of that time, and it landed me a job as an instructor in a small Massachusetts state college.

There I had the thrill of being the young radical professor and introducing rural kids, more than half of whom had never been to Boston 40 miles away, to Gary Snyder, Native American poetry, and the destructive political ideas that were then hypercharging our country.
The first-ever trip to California, and here to Washington, that summer of 1969 blew the door off that first right livelihood endeavor.
I was offered a job to build houses on Whidbey Island for the following year.
I tendered my resignation, taught one more year, and headed west, where I discovered the joys of carpentry, out-of-door labor, and living in my body in ways academia and lab work never provided.

Two years in beach houses followed by four years of apprenticing and working as a commercial wooden boat builder in Vancouver made me certain I had found a way to put a roof over my head, feed my young family, and continue a specialized trade with mythic roots and real life and death outcomes.
I had found it, or so I thought.
Then a story in the local Anacortes paper about nearby Hart Lake, threatened by condominium development, embroiled me as an advocate for preservation.

Meanwhile, I was fully devoted to my work repairing salmon fishing boats for Puget Sound in Alaska, not quite recognizing, at that time, my facilitating role in accelerating the near elimination of our benchmark ecosystem linchpin, while also using prime two-inch thick edge-grain old-growth Douglas fir to plank the hulls of these boats.
Down on the floats one rainy February day, putting a new flying bridge on an Alaska-bound fish boat, cold and tired, the question arose: do you want to be doing this 20 years from now?
Then a few months later, a state parks planner watching me chair a meeting for the future city of Anacortes forest land said, "I have a lot of interns coming through my shop.
You're good at this.
You should go back to school and do this professionally."
A summer fishing for salmon around Kodiak Island aboard a 42-foot boat I had helped rebuild financed my way back to UW Graduate School.

I loved the fishing life, but an internship with DNR the next summer began a 12-year period of large-scale statewide forest land conservation, including protecting many areas of old-growth forest ecosystems in Skagit, Whatcom, and San Juan counties.
The Natural Resource Conservation Areas Act, which I researched, drafted, and successfully lobbied the bill for, now encompasses some 125,000 acres.
I calculated that out to about 200 square miles.
Over the past 24 years, the state has [unclear: "appropriate"] over $750 million to permanently protect these heritage lands.
The southern end of Lummi Island, 90% of Cypress Island, and the Lake Louise section of the Stimson Preserve are some local examples of these now protected areas.
Sadly, as the land commissioner's 12-year term was ending, my mom passed away, just as I was about to go to work for the Nature Conservancy.
Instead, my then-wife, a family doc and brilliant horticulturist, and I purchased a small four-acre farm east of La Conner, where she grew native [unclear: "boas"].
I developed a specialty vegetable farm, supplying restaurants and the Anacortes Farmer's Market.
Classic right livelihood: hard work, low pay, growing beautiful organic vegetables with views of Mt.
Baker and Mt.
Erie.
Then a leading local farmer asked if I would serve on the board of the small, nonprofit farmland organization, Skagitonians to Preserve Farmland.
The director soon took a job with Cascadian Farms, and I stepped in on a one-day-a-week contract.

Twelve years later, working more than full-time with a staff of three, I retired after spearheading the effort to create a [unclear: "purchase of a development program"] that now permanently protects more than 14,000 acres of some of the best farmland in the world.
It also sparked the $8 million effort to rebuild the WSU research station facility and protect the surrounding farmland.
Various consulting jobs followed, including working with the Skagit Farmer's Group, making the best pickles and sauerkraut ever.
And sadly, they went out of business because of bad financing.
But I got their organic sauerkraut into whole food markets, and then they tanked.
It was really a sad story.
One thing led to another, and ten years ago, I began working on a project for a local sawmill that manufactures musical instrument-quality wood.
They partnered with a major guitar maker to ensure the long-term stability and supply of koa, a beautiful and unique wood to the Hawaiian Islands.

We've had great success and are now using harvest revenues to rebuild the native forest through fencing to eliminate destructive cattle, sheep, and pig degradation, and fostering regeneration of the complex understory species that will help rebuild and restore forest ecosystems rather than simply creating new monoculture plantations.
Each of these jobs, vocations, opportunities interconnected me to the world in complex ways.
It was impossible to separate that work from the inherent impurities we live within, but I rarely found myself questioning the basic goodness of what I was doing.
Sure, there were difficult days, legislative failures, unsuccessful negotiations, problematic employees, working on the docks in the rain and in the field on a hot summer day.
But in retrospect, the overall outcomes were the beautiful basil for the farmer's market, a well-fit plank on a boat hull, or passing a local ordinance to protect farmland.
I can view all of that as right livelihood.

Impossible to say how causes and conditions all brought this to pass, but my current practice tells me that dumb luck, intuition, and some appropriate choices in response to conditions made this all possible, for which I feel most blessed and fortunate.
In my readings to prepare this talk, I found an appropriate closing quotation from a core Vipassana teacher, S.
N.
Goenka.
*If the intention is to play a useful role in society in order to support oneself and to help others, then the work one does is right livelihood.*
So I leave you with a question to ponder: is your work, or the way you think, speak, and act at work, benefiting others or causing harm?
What I suggest is that we break out into groups of four and take a few minutes to ponder these questions, which are all interrelated.
What about your current work embodies right livelihood?
What about your current work is not right livelihood?
What changes could you make to bring your work closer to right livelihood?
What's getting in the way?
We'll break into groups of four and have a little conversation, and then we'll come back and have just a one or two liner from each group to reflect on our lives with right livelihood.
And you guys could be, oh, Neil had to leave.
I guess it's you and Bob, Desiree.
You're a group of two.
Okay.
Can you hear me?
Yeah.
Yeah, everybody else left.
Well, that was really, really a great talk.
I was thinking it's just so fun to hear the stories too, and how everything flowed from one thing into the next thing.

But as you were talking, this is not about me, this is about you, I was thinking that part of that right livelihood that I saw in whatever you were doing, mostly working in the kitchen, and those are, can you hear me?
Tim's going to turn down a little bit.
Yeah.
Oh, sorry.

I was thinking about how much the person's efforts themselves, I guess you could say right effort, interact with the right livelihood, because I was really amazed when I used to watch you preparing the food in the kitchen, the small kitchen over there on Forest.
Right.
Always optimistic.
I never saw any complaining or disgruntled anything.
And I really appreciated that.
I feel like that's something surely that you have brought to all of these different endeavors, and I think that's a really important piece of right livelihood.

Well, it's interesting you say that, because there was a point in my life early on when I came to the conclusion that if I had enough energy to complain, I had enough energy to try to do something about it, so I don't complain.
And it's actually served me well because it avoids getting into all kinds of negative thinking.
Yeah.

In the kitchen, I've talked to Tim a little bit about this, but working on a 42-foot fishing boat feeding four people with a tiny, not much to cook with, it makes you a very different kind of cook, where you have to clean up as you go along and everything, and essentially being the tenzo on a fishing boat.
And I learned a lot from that experience that summer, being with some not very attractive people really, people who I would never have been with otherwise.
They were my crew and I had to put up with them.
Interesting.
Yeah.
Well, I was thinking about myself, and I worked for many years in the medical community and I did a lot of education with patients.
Right.
And I always felt that that was good work.
I felt like that was right livelihood.
I enjoyed what I did.
I felt like I was being helpful and useful.
But I also feel like there could have been a time where I had more courage to get into work with the environment and with all the species on this earth.
And I feel like that was something I just didn't have the courage for.
It was one thing to work with people in this medical community and feel like I was being useful, but it felt more scary for me to really move into an area that took a lot of.
I felt like it took a lot of courage, and I admire these people that do that kind of work.
Pardon me?
Advocacy for the environment kind of work.
Yeah, yeah.
And the environment and all of the living things, that's a big passion.
And I felt like at the time I wanted to do that, but I didn't have the courage to do that.
So I moved into this other work that I thought, okay, this is good.
But it wasn't my passion, in that way that I could have done earlier.
Well, that advocacy work for the environment is how much time you spend in hearings and meetings.

And you're trying to fight or support rules and regulations that are going to help the environment, fighting against those who want to use the environment in a very different way than you have in mind.
So it requires, as I've learned, a lot of patience and patience.
And oftentimes your gains are sometimes temporary and [unclear: "finding permanent"].
That's why I like things like buying development rights, because it's a property interest that's actually defended.
It's not just a policy or an idea that can fall apart because different politicians come in or things like that.
And of course, that isn't my favorite kind of work.
So my ideal was there, but the actual work probably would not have been something that I could have been of great benefit doing, I think.
Yeah, I think a lot of it is because I have a hard time with conflict, and there would have been a lot of conflict, of course, within those realms of things that I have so much passion for.
So anyway, it's really interesting to think about the paths we choose: what part of that was right livelihood that I felt good about, and what part of it may have been.
I could have maybe taken a little bit more, gotten in there a little bit more with the things that I had a passion for.
I mean, from my senses, I went to this meeting about Heart Lake at the house, but [unclear: "part past late by deception passed"] and I got involved.
All of a sudden my whole life changed, one step, and as I said, I opened the door and it fell down an elevator shaft.
It felt like, yeah, I thought being an environmentalist was reading Gary Snyder poetry.
Yeah, well, but that's not the action.
That's the idea.
So, yeah, right.
Hard part.
Yeah.
I think as I get older I have more courage to just get in and do the work.
But it was really interesting.
I had just actually switched my master's to Antioch in Seattle.
I was going to do this degree in environment community.
So I finally did jump into that.
And then we decided, oh my gosh, we need to adopt our son if we're ever going to do it now.
And everything shifted, which I don't regret at all.
But yeah, interesting.
Trying to be the moderator and timekeeper at the same time.
Anyway, I really enjoyed the talk.
Go ahead.
You opened us up to the heart of the Buddhist teachings.
I find it a very helpful book.
I began reading there and then other things.
I'm glad.
It seemed like it opened people up to different things, and it was good timing somehow, I think.
So interesting, how you start reading the Eightfold Path and the precepts.
I haven't seen the text that sort of shows how they relate to each other, per se.
But they reflect back and forth on each other.
They do.
How to behave.
I love that [unclear: "Siddhant Han"] likes using the phrase of being polite.
Being sort of respecting each other, respecting the earth.
Conducting yourself properly.
I think it's a really profound notion we forget about sometimes.
Yeah, I think we really struggle with that.
In this country right now, there are so many other energies coming up.
So I just feel like we need to do the best that we can in this honest way.
It's a karmic task.
Yeah, it is.
It's never going to happen, so.
I'm really glad you joined us for tonight.
I know you couldn't make it.
Yes.
I'm glad too.
I think Bert's listening in the other room too.
Sorry.
I have a little audience.
Well, I think what we're going to do is have our little [unclear: "feedback moves"] here.
It's about a quarter of nine.
Right.
Thank you.
Thank you. [unclear: "Take your job on the move and do all this."] Finally, when I started sitting with Ruth Seager, she said that to me one time.
And I said, I can't.
When I'm showering, I'm supposed to be showering, not thinking about how to [unclear: "revise the computer to the elements"].
But what I've been thinking about is, as Scott was talking about, I really probably did.
My second teacher, she was very much in the prison world.
So I spent three years going to a [unclear: "mass prison"] in Missouri.
And there was a lot of things going on there.
So she would build.
So all this.
Nice job getting us talking.
Good.
Just a couple of minutes to wrap up.
Yeah, yeah.
You're done.
I'm pretty much on time.
I've heard your job history several times.
It amazes me every time.
It probably amazes you too.
It does.
I left out a bunch of stuff too.
Well, it appears maybe I should have spoken less and let you speak more, because everyone seems to be involved in some very intensive conversations.
Let's take a second.
I'm not sure if each group has something to say or someone from each group wants to say something.
But the floor is open for a few comments before we close for the evening.
Start over here.
Just a little group here.
Any comments?
Well, I'll tell you the way we ended.
We ended by saying it's okay to say no.
Just say no.
Just say no.
You guys did a great one.

Someone had this idea that one of us talked about a very impressive boss and struggling with this person who would try and give tasks. [unclear: "Is there a game I can tell you a story you want to tell?"] I can tell a story.
You tell it.
I had a boss that would always tell us to work on something at home or think about this while you're in the shower, or this weekend if he has some extra time, work on this, work on that.
And when I started formally practicing with Red Cedar, I turned to her the next time she said it.
And I said, no, it's against my religion.
When I'm showering, I'm supposed to be showering.
Just say no.
Also, it's against my religion.
I know.
Oh my gosh, I forgot.
Other comments from Jeff and your group over there?
Any comments or thoughts?
Just for myself, I'm retired, so I started thinking, what about now?
In that formal sense, I don't have something more like right living or right.
Carrie, your group back there, any thoughts?
We've talked about different transitional phases in our lives and how we're going to resonate with fields that we didn't really want to be in and what to do about that.
So what it came down to is another question: what is the definition of work in certain circumstances, and then also the joy of creating your own.
So I think we ended up with the question, what can we create for ourselves?

I think that in terms of how to actually put those nuts and bolts together in our daily life, this is the way it is, regardless of what we've done in the past, but to go forward with a creative attitude.
Thank you.
You're the person back there?
I think that as I reflect on each person's speaking, what we came up with is it's complicated.
Because every theoretically right livelihood brings with it all the underside of the log.
For each one of us who work in what I would call a path of noble effort, there are all these things that constrain or negate, or it's not easy.
So that's my summary of our group, and then I guess my own: maybe employ some forbearance and say it's somewhere and it's worth it.
Saying no to others and saying no to ourselves is both saying no.
John?
Scott?
One of the things is, with all of the problems in the world with homelessness and all the ecological problems, it's hard to feel like you're doing enough for those problems.
You could of course burn yourself out completely.
So the idea, especially for people that have jobs, that's a big time and energy commitment right there.
And then there's how much energy you put in on top of that to help all these problems that are going on in the world.
As a retired person, for me, I look more at how I spend my time so that I can look back on a day and feel like I've got some things done, I did some things that were beneficial.
And I also had some time to do what I want to do, and I try to keep that in mind every day.
Thank you all.
Wise comments all around.
Bob, can I say one thing real quick?
Desiree, yeah.
Can you hear?
Yeah, I just wanted to say that as I was listening to Bob's talk, I thought how much right livelihood involves right effort, too.
Everyone's livelihood, no matter what it is, really is influenced so much by the effort of the person themselves.
As Bob was talking, I was thinking about him modeling for us in the kitchen those years at Forest, in this little tiny kitchen, putting together these meals for everybody.
I never heard any complaining.
He never seemed flustered with putting meals together in this little tiny place that you could barely even stand in, for all these people.
I was really joyful reflecting on that and thinking about the effort that we can put in for right livelihood, no matter what that is.
Anyway, it was just a really nice memory to remember and have modeled.
So thanks, Bob.
You learn a lot from cooking for four people on a 42-foot fishing boat for a summer in Alaska.
To a more prolonged period of practice.
What are the times?

verbatim.text: New friends, nice to see everyone. Old friends and new faces. A few months ago, we took on, some of us took on an assignment to take one of the Eightfold Noble Path portions and speak to that, and I chose Right Livelihood, which might also be called Ethics of Earning a Living or Conscious Livelihood, and I want to begin by acknowledging Scott Allen's presentation on the same topic a few weeks ago, some wires got crossed, and so we both did the same thing, and to appreciate Scott's openness to address the dilemma that he walked through of integrating Right Livelihood in the context of military service. I listened to his talk after I had begun preparation for my assignment that I had penned months ago, so there may be a few items repeated, but hopefully I'll cover some new ground and remind us all of how central this concept of Right Livelihood is for maintaining the integrity of our lives of continuing practice in this chaotic and changing world we live in. I'll open up with a few initial reflections, followed by a brief overview of what the Buddha offers as teachings on Right Livelihood, and conclude, as Tim asked us to, with some reflections on how our personal stories, or at least my imagination of that story, provide some examples of what can be considered, I think, Right Livelihood. Then I'd like to take a few minutes for all of us to reflect on this intersection of our practice and our day-to-day lives. So in Pali, this element is called Samo Adjivo, commonly translated as Right Livelihood, but if you dig a little bit deeper, it's clear that this term means more than a job to make money to put a roof over your head, to buy food, to have clothes and secure medicine. In Pali, the prefix sama means complete or perfected, rather than right with all its connotations of orthodox correctness. Samo Adjivo might better be translated more like Livelihood fully understood and rightly conducted within all the tensions of our lives.

Thich Nhat Hanh reminds us in the heart of the Buddha's teaching, the text that Desiree so beautifully guided us through, that it is not possible to practice one element of the Noble Eightfold Path without practicing all seven other elements. This is the nature of interbeing, and it is true for all the teachings offered by the Buddha. He continues to practice Right Livelihood, you have to find a way to earn your living without transgressing your ideals of love and compassion. The way you support yourself can be an expression of your deepest self, or it can be a source of suffering for you and others. Our vocation can nourish our understanding and compassion, or erode them. We should be awake to the consequences far and near of the way we earn our living. In this perspective, another way to view Right Livelihood is to live in ways that contribute to harmony and well-being in nature and society, in our relationships with each other, and with the entire web of life. A group of us have been studying the precepts, and I've been reminded how the Three Pure Precepts essentially offer us a high-level perspective on practicing Right Livelihood in our day-to-day lives.

Do good, avoid causing harm, and help others. It really comes down to making our best effort, despite difficulties, moment by moment, breath by breath, to fully embody these guideposts. As we consider Right Livelihood tonight, I'd like you to reflect on a few lines from the Metta Sutta about Right Livelihood in the context of how we live our lives in our current social context. We chant, This is what should be accomplished by the one who is wise. Let one be strenuous, upright, and sincere, without pride, easily contented, and joyous. Let one not be submerged by the things of the world. Let one not take on the burden of riches. Let one's senses be controlled.

And let one be wise, but not puffed up, and let one not desire great possessions even for one's family. We will investigate this further. These lines are a good reminder that it's not only a matter of how we earn our living, but also of what we do and what is affected by our securing those resources. Then what we do with those resources and how we use them to present ourselves within our larger community of family, sangha, and mother earth sangha, because of our ability to access material wealth. The eightfold path elements are not so much prescriptions for behavior as qualities, a framework present in the mind of a person on the enlightening path. Committed to ending suffering for all beings. One classic way that's used to see the structure of these eight interrelated path elements is to view them as a threefold training in ethics, concentration, and wisdom. Ethics or avoidance of non-virtuous deeds through right speech, right action, and right livelihood.

Concentration or control of the mind through right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. And wisdom or the development of insight into the nature of reality as right view and right intention. What the Buddha taught about right and wrong livelihood for the mainly rural society he lived was pro-bit-pro-bit. What the Buddha taught about right and wrong livelihood for the mainly rural society he lived was pro-bit-prohibitory. In that he said lay people shouldn't engage in five specific types of business. Dealing in weapons. Trade in human beings, i.e. slavery and prostitution, although some translations say trade in any beings, human and non-human. Meat production and butchery as a trade not as a necessity of individual survival.

Business and intoxicants and business and poisons. He also, the Buddha also when pressed vigorously three questions asked by senior monks. He cautioned against becoming a soldier, quote, because the mind is already seized, debased, and misdirected by the thought may these beings be struck down or slaughtered or annihilated or destroyed. In the Digya Nikaya Sutra, the Buddha extensively lays out prohibitions for monks and by inference but for seriously practicing lay people.

In the Anuttara Sutra, the Buddha reflects on the Middle Way when he tells disciple Vyajra Habaja, a householder knowing his income and expenses leads a balanced life. He uses the image of a goldsmith holding up a balance scale, who knows how much it is tilted or dipped down to know the right balance point. Each of us is that goldsmith, monitoring our behavior, knowing when we are tilting toward imbalance, and hopefully self-correcting to keep our lives properly in balance. Beyond a balancing of income and expense for the necessities of life is the question of one's attitude towards consumption and how we view what we need versus our wants. This is a deep systemic dilemma we all face every day in the context of global, exploitive, market-driven, hyper-consumer-based capitalism perfected right here in America.

One of the Buddha's teachings is to let go of our acquisitive tendencies, which thereby weakens our temptation to engage in wrong livelihood in order to secure more than we need for reasonable comfort in our lives. Or as Bodhidharma counsels in his outline of practice, accept conditions and want nothing. Taking a moment to reflect each time our mind signals a want in the face of endless temptations, many of which require a financial response, is a critical exercise in understanding what we truly need to meet our basic requirements of living as conscious lay people in this increasingly complex, technology-driven 21st century.
